title: Roles of the Nurse in Peri-operative Care
path: Roles of the Nurse in Peri-operative Care

headings.title: Introduction to Peri-operative Nursing
headings.content: Peri-operative nursing encompasses the care provided to patients before, during, and after surgical and invasive procedures. As a critical component of the healthcare team in Nigeria and globally, peri-operative nurses ensure that patients transition through the surgical journey safely and effectively. This specialized field requires a deep understanding of human anatomy, physiology, pharmacology, and sterile techniques. The peri-operative continuum is traditionally divided into three distinct phases: the pre-operative phase, the intra-operative phase, and the post-operative phase. In each of these phases, the nurse assumes multifaceted roles, acting as a direct caregiver, educator, coordinator, and fierce advocate for the patient. By assessing risks, preparing the surgical environment, monitoring vital signs, and preventing complications, peri-operative nurses significantly improve surgical outcomes and reduce mortality and morbidity rates. Nigerian nursing students must master these foundational concepts to meet the rigorous standards set by the Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria (NMCN) and to deliver holistic, evidence-based care in diverse clinical settings, ranging from primary health centers to tertiary teaching hospitals.

headings.title: Pre-operative
headings.content: The pre-operative phase begins when the decision for surgical intervention is made and ends when the patient is transferred to the operating room table. During this critical time, the nurse conducts a comprehensive baseline assessment, which includes taking a detailed medical history, conducting physical examinations, reviewing laboratory and diagnostic results, and assessing psychological readiness and anxiety levels. Patient education is a cornerstone of pre-operative nursing; nurses must explain what to expect during surgery, teach deep breathing and coughing exercises, demonstrate early ambulation techniques, and discuss pain management strategies. Informed consent verification is another paramount duty. The nurse must ensure that the surgical consent form has been voluntarily signed by a competent adult patient after the surgeon has adequately explained the procedure, risks, and benefits, acting primarily as a witness to the signature. Furthermore, physical preparation involves surgical site marking, skin cleansing, fasting (NPO status) verification, and administering pre-anesthetic medications as ordered. Identifying and documenting known allergies, previous anesthetic complications, and current medications helps mitigate potential risks before the patient enters the theater.

headings.title: Intra-operative
headings.content: The intra-operative phase spans from the time the patient is transferred to the operating room table until they are admitted to the Post-Anesthesia Care Unit (PACU). Within the operating theater, nursing roles are broadly categorized into two distinct functions: scrub nursing and circulating nursing. The scrub nurse maintains the sterile field, assists the surgeon by handling instruments, sutures, and supplies, and performs accurate sponge, needle, and instrument counts alongside the circulating nurse. Conversely, the circulating nurse remains non-sterile, managing the overall operating room environment, coordinating activities, managing specimen collections, documenting intra-operative events, and ensuring patient safety measures such as correct positioning and grounding pad placement for electrosurgery. Both roles require meticulous attention to maintaining strict aseptic technique to prevent surgical site infections. Additionally, the intra-operative nurse monitors the patient's physiological status in collaboration with the anesthetist or anesthesiologist, observing for adverse reactions such as malignant hyperthermia, blood loss, or hemodynamic instability. Team communication using standardized tools like surgical time-outs is vital to prevent wrong-site, wrong-procedure, or wrong-person surgery.

headings.title: Post-operative
headings.content: The post-operative phase begins immediately after surgery and concludes when the patient has achieved complete recovery from the surgical intervention, which may extend through follow-up visits in the community. Initially, care is delivered in the Post-Anesthesia Care Unit (PACU) or surgical intensive care unit, where the primary focus is monitoring vital signs, maintaining a patent airway, managing pain, and monitoring for hemorrhage or shock. The PACU nurse performs frequent assessments of respiratory status, oxygen saturation, neurological function, and surgical site drainage. As the patient stabilizes, they are transferred back to the surgical ward or discharged home. In the ward, the nurse continues to monitor for post-operative complications such as deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism, urinary retention, surgical site infections, and paralytic ileus. Nursing interventions focus heavily on promoting early ambulation, incentive spirometry, adequate hydration and nutrition, and meticulous wound care. Discharge planning begins early in the peri-operative process and includes educating the patient and their family members on medication regimens, activity restrictions, dietary modifications, and recognizing red-flag symptoms that necessitate immediate medical attention.

headings.title: Patient Safety and Advocacy Across the Peri-operative Continuum
headings.content: Patient safety and advocacy are central tenets of peri-operative nursing practice across all phases of care. Because surgical patients are often vulnerable, unresponsive, or heavily medicated, nurses must act as their steadfast advocates to protect their rights, dignity, and physical safety. This advocacy involves verifying patient identity using multiple identifiers, ensuring correct surgical site marking, enforcing strict adherence to sterile protocols, and preventing accidental retained surgical items through meticulous counts. Furthermore, safety encompasses environmental hazards management in the operating theater and ward, such as checking electrical equipment safety, preventing patient falls, and protecting pressure areas during prolonged surgical positioning. Nurses also advocate for patient autonomy by ensuring that patients are fully informed and that their expressed wishes regarding treatment limitations are respected. In Nigerian clinical settings, where resource constraints can sometimes challenge ideal practices, the nurse's commitment to safety and advocacy becomes even more critical in preventing adverse events, reducing hospital stay lengths, and saving lives through vigilance and adherence to international and national safety checklists.

headings.title: Documentation and Legal Ethical Considerations in Peri-operative Care
headings.content: Documentation and legal-ethical considerations are fundamental responsibilities that protect both the patient and the nursing professional. Accurate, objective, and timely documentation is required across the pre-operative, intra-operative, and post-operative phases to maintain a clear legal record of care. Nurses must document patient assessments, nursing diagnoses, interventions, patient responses, and communications with other members of the healthcare team. In accordance with legal and professional guidelines in Nigeria, charting must be legible, contemporaneous, and devoid of personal opinions or alterations. Legally, peri-operative nurses are bound by the scope of practice defined by the Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria and must operate within their legal boundaries to avoid malpractice or negligence claims. Ethical principles such as beneficence (doing good), non-maleficence (doing no harm), autonomy (respecting patient choices), and justice must guide every clinical decision. Confidentiality is also paramount; patient health information must be safeguarded under professional codes of conduct. Understanding these legal and ethical obligations empowers student nurses to practice safely, respect human rights, and navigate complex clinical scenarios with professional integrity.
